title: Retail and Trade Management
summary: Learn to run a profitable shop or trading business: retail formats and location, merchandising, markup and margin, shrinkage, stock control, sales drivers and service, cash handling, digital payments and selling online.
audience: Shop owners, traders, retail staff and business students

lessons.title: Retail formats and the trader's role

body.p: Retail is selling goods to final consumers. It ranges from street vendors and spaza shops to supermarkets, pharmacies, fashion chains and online stores. Wholesale sells in bulk to retailers and other businesses. Retailers add value by choosing the right range, buying in bulk, storing goods, offering convenience and advice, and providing credit or delivery.

list: Informal traders and market stalls: low costs, flexible hours, close customer relationships.
Convenience and neighbourhood shops: small range, close to home, open long hours.
Supermarkets and hypermarkets: wide range, self-service, low prices through volume.
Specialist stores: focused ranges and expert advice, such as electronics or pharmacies.
Franchises: an independent owner runs a store under an established brand and system.
Online and omnichannel: selling through websites, social media and apps, often combined with physical stores.

body.p: Location remains crucial for physical shops: foot traffic, visibility, parking or transport links, security and competition all shape sales.

body.tip: Before opening, count passers-by at different times of day and note which competitors they visit.

body.p: Merchandising is how products are chosen, displayed and promoted to encourage buying. A well-organised shop helps customers find what they need and discover more.

list: Place essentials (bread, milk) towards the back so customers pass other products.
Put high-margin and impulse items at eye level and near the till.
Group related products together (pasta with sauces).
Keep shelves full, clean and clearly priced; empty gaps lose sales.
Use the front of the shop for promotions and new arrivals.
Rotate stock so older items (by expiry date) sell first.

body.p: Choose a range that fits your customers: breadth (how many categories) and depth (how many options within each). A small shop cannot stock everything, so focus on items that sell reliably and add a few that attract customers in, such as fresh bread.

body.tip: Stand where customers enter and look at the shop through their eyes. What do they see first, and is it what you want to sell?

body.p: Retailers must understand the difference between markup and margin. If an item costs R100 and sells for R150, the markup on cost is 50 / 100 = 50%, but the gross margin on the selling price is 50 / 150, about 33.3%. Confusing the two leads to prices that are too low.

A 20% discount on that R150 item brings the price to R120. The margin falls from R50 to R20, or about 16.7% of the new price, so many more units must be sold to earn the same profit. Use promotions with a clear purpose, such as clearing old stock or attracting new customers.

Shrinkage is stock lost through theft, damage, spoilage and administrative errors. A shop with R2 000 000 of annual sales and 1.5% shrinkage loses R30 000 a year. Controls include good layout and visibility, staff training, regular stock counts, careful receiving of deliveries and secure cash handling.

body.tip: Check every delivery against the invoice before the supplier leaves; errors found later are hard to recover.

body.p: Stock is cash sitting on shelves. Buy too little and you lose sales; buy too much and money is tied up, goods expire and space runs out.

list: Stock turn: cost of sales divided by average stock. R600 000 cost of sales with R150 000 average stock is 600 000 / 150 000 = 4 turns a year, about 3 months of stock.
Sell-through rate: units sold divided by units received. Selling 80 of 100 shirts is 80%.
Days of cover: how long current stock will last at the current selling rate.
Fast and slow movers: identify both; reorder the fast, reduce or clear the slow.
Use sales records to forecast demand, including seasonal peaks such as school opening and festive seasons.
Negotiate prices, payment terms and delivery with several suppliers.
Join buying groups or cooperatives to get bulk prices.
Use a simple point-of-sale system or app to track sales and stock in real time.

body.tip: Review your slowest-selling 20 items every month and decide: promote, reduce or stop stocking.

body.p: Retail sales can be broken into three drivers: sales = footfall x conversion rate x average transaction value. If 1200 people visit in a week, 300 buy (conversion 300 / 1200 = 25%) and the average sale is R300, weekly sales are 1200 x 0.25 x 300 = R90 000. Raising conversion to 30% with the same footfall and basket adds sales of 1200 x 0.30 x 300 = R108 000.

list: Footfall: visibility, signage, promotions, social media and good opening hours.
Conversion: product availability, helpful staff, short queues and easy payment, including cards and mobile money.
Transaction value: suggest related items, offer bundles and stock quality options.
Greet customers and be available without pressuring them.
Know the products and stock levels.
Handle complaints calmly; refund or replace as consumer law requires.
Remember regular customers and their preferences.

body.tip: Count visitors and transactions for one week; knowing your conversion rate shows where to focus.

body.p: Good cash management keeps a retail business alive. Separate business and personal money, bank takings regularly, and reconcile the till at the end of each day: opening float plus cash sales should equal cash in the till.

list: Card machines and mobile money (such as M-Pesa, MTN MoMo and others) reduce cash risk and attract customers without cash.
Compare transaction fees and settlement times between providers.
Keep records of every transaction; they also help when applying for loans.
Watch for payment scams, such as fake payment-confirmation messages; confirm receipt in your own account before handing over goods.

body.p: Many small retailers start with social media and messaging apps: post photos and prices, take orders by message and deliver locally. Next steps include online marketplaces and simple online stores. Online selling needs accurate stock information, clear delivery and returns policies, good photos and quick replies.

body.tip: Never release goods because of a screenshot or SMS alone; check that the money has actually arrived in your account.
